title: Integrated Security & Compliance Controlbook: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency, SDLC, Incident Response, Evidence Workflows
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Summary:
This document consolidates Redwood Inference's security and compliance controls for access (RBAC & authentication), audit logging, data residency and retention, secure software development lifecycle (SDLC) practices, incident response for security events, compliance evidence collection workflows, and risk/exception handling. It is intended as the authoritative controlbook for engineering, security, and compliance teams when onboarding customers, responding to audits, or implementing new features that affect trust and data governance.

Scope:
- Applies to all Redwood-managed control plane and inference control surfaces (hosted API, Dedicated control plane, and Private control plane integrations).
- Includes developer-facing APIs, internal admin consoles, observability pipelines, and customer telemetry collectors.
- Excludes third-party vendor policies except where explicitly referenced in supply-chain evidence.

Principles:
- Least privilege: grant minimum permissions necessary; prefer role-based and time-limited grants over broad service accounts.
- Auditability: all privileged actions must be traceable to an identity with immutable audit logs retained per retention policy.
- Data residency & minimization: store customer data only in approved regions and for the minimum required retention period.
- Defensible SDLC: security gates, automated checks, and evidence artifacts must be reproducible for audits.
- Timely response: security incidents should be triaged and escalated with clear SLAs and evidence preservation.

1) RBAC & Authentication
Overview:
Redwood uses centralized identity and access management for both human and service principals. We enforce role-based access controls (RBAC) layered with multi-factor authentication (MFA) for interactive logins and short-lived credentials for services.

Key roles and responsibilities:
- Security Admin (security team): owns global RBAC model, role definitions, and privileged access reviews (quarterly).
- Platform Owner (eng-platform): implements role enforcement in the console and API gateway.
- Service Owner (product/engineering): responsible for least-privilege role maps for their service.

Authentication and identity flows:
- Human users: SSO (OIDC) via corporate IdP; MFA (TOTP + hardware key for admins); SCIM provisioning for role sync.
- Services: short-lived certificates/STS tokens issued by the internal token service. All service tokens expire within 24 hours by default; higher-risk operations require step-up delegation.

RBAC controls and examples (table):
| Role | Typical members | Privileges | Review cadence |
| Security Admin | security@redwood.com | Create roles, approve exceptions, view all audit logs | Quarterly |
| Platform Operator | eng-platform | Deploy, scale, manage runtime configuration | Monthly |
| Customer Support | customer-success | Read-only customer metadata, masked logs | Monthly |
| Billing Agent | finance-legal | Billing reports, invoices | Quarterly |

Provisioning and deprovisioning:
1. New hire onboarding: SCIM creates base role 'employee' and assigns team-specific roles via manager approval.
2. Leavers: HR webhook triggers immediate suspension of account, token revocation, and access review.
3. Emergency access (break-glass): time-limited (max 8 hours), logged, and requires post-incident review.

2) Audit Logging
Requirements:
- All privileged actions (role changes, config updates, deployment rollouts, RBAC exceptions, access to customer data) must generate immutable audit events.
- Audit records MUST include: timestamp (UTC, RFC3339), actor_id, actor_role, action, target_resource, request_id, outcome (success/failure), and correlation_id when applicable.
- Logs are shipped to the centralized observability cluster with write-once retention and tamper-evident integrity (hash chaining).

Retention and SLOs:
- Real-time retention: hot logs stored for 90 days for operational troubleshooting.
- Warm retention: 1 year for compliance investigations.
- Cold archival: 7 years for regulated customer contracts (when required).
- SLO: audit pipeline must deliver 99.9% of events to the archive within 10 minutes of generation. Any delivery failure >1 hour triggers an alert to on-call security.

Access controls for logs:
- Role-based access: only authorized roles can query raw audit logs; support and platform teams receive masked views by default.
- Evidence snapshots: for audits, security can create signed snapshots (ZIP + manifest) with a chain-of-custody record.

3) Data Residency & Retention
Policy:
- Customer data classification: PII, non-PII, model artifacts, and telemetry. Each classification maps to allowed regions and retention.
- Default deployment region is based on customer contract; cross-region replication requires explicit customer consent and contract annotation.

Retention matrix (example):
| Data type | Default retention | Archive option | Notes |
| Logs (operational) | 90 days hot / 1 year warm | 7 years archival (contractual) | Mask sensitive fields by default |
| Customer request payloads | 30 days | 90 days with consent | Redact PII unless customer enables recording |
| Embeddings & derived artifacts | 90 days | Customer-configurable | Customers can opt-out of storage |
| Model binaries | Indefinite (versioned) | N/A | Access controlled via RBAC |

Implementation checklist:
- Ensure region tags on every storage bucket and DB instance.
- Automated purge jobs run nightly; retention failures escalate to data-ops.
- Encryption at rest using KMS keys; customer-managed keys available for Private deployments.

4) Secure SDLC
Gates and tooling:
- Threat modeling required for all services touching customer data; documented with mitigations in PRD.
- Mandatory presubmit checks: static analysis (SAST), dependency scanning (SCA), secret scanning, and license checks.
- CI pipeline must run container image scanning and dynamic application security testing (DAST) for public-facing endpoints.
- Security review required for high-privilege changes (RBAC, auth flows, logging changes).

Artefacts to generate per release:
- Build manifest (artifact hashes), SBOM (Software Bill of Materials), test coverage report, vulnerability scan summary, and threat model updates.
- Release approver (product/security) must sign off for production rollouts.

5) Incident Response  Security Events
Triage and escalation:
- Incident severity levels: Sev3 (informational), Sev2 (service-impacting), Sev1 (security compromise or data exfiltration).
- Detection: automated alerts from IDS/IPS, anomaly detection in audit logs, customer reports, and third-party breach notifications.

Initial response steps (numbered):
1. Triage: on-call security reviews alerts within 15 minutes for Sev1/2.
2. Containment: apply scoped mitigations (token revocation, network ACL update, isolate compute).
3. Evidence preservation: snapshot affected VMs, preserve audit logs, freeze deletion and retention jobs for affected resources.
4. Communication: notify incident-comm team; prepare customer-safe summary within 4 hours for Sev1 affecting customer data.
5. Recovery and remediation: patch, rotate keys, and validate fixes via regression tests.
6. Post-incident review: within 7 days, produce a postmortem with root cause, timeline, and action items.

Evidence preservation requirements:
- Chain-of-custody recorded for all collected artifacts.
- Tamper-evident storage for preserved artifacts.
- For regulatory incidents, preserve artifacts for the longer of contractual or legal retention periods.

6) Compliance Evidence Workflows
Workflow overview:
- Evidence intake: automation collects SBOM, build manifests, audit snapshots, role review logs, and signed approvals.
- Evidence tagging: each artifact is tagged with customer_id (when applicable), control_id (SOC2/ISO control mapping), and timestamp.
- Request process: internal audit or customer compliance requests are submitted through the compliance ticket queue (Jira).

Deliverables and SLAs:
- SOC2 evidence requests responded within 10 business days by default; expedited tracks available for high-priority customers.
- Evidence packages include a manifest, hashes, and reviewer attestations.

7) Risk and Exceptions
Risk acceptance and exception process:
1. Any deviation from documented controls requires a formal exception request in the risk register.
2. Request must include: description, compensating controls, impacted assets, time-bound duration (max 90 days), and owner.
3. Approval levels: service owner -> security -> CRO for high-risk; exceptions >90 days require board-level visibility.

Periodic review and mitigation:
- Exceptions are reviewed monthly; mitigations and sunset plans tracked.
- High-risk exceptions trigger mandatory compensating controls (increased monitoring, reduced blast radius).

Appendices:
A. Contact and ownership table:
- Security Pager: sec-oncall@redwood.com (Primary)
- Compliance & Audit: compliance@redwood.com
- Platform Owner: eng-platform@redwood.com
- Data-ops: data-ops@redwood.com

B. Sample CLI commands for evidence snapshot:
- Create snapshot: redwoodctl evidence snapshot --service <service> --since 2028-10-01 --out /tmp/evidence.zip
- Verify manifest: sha256sum -c evidence_manifest.sha256

C. Change log highlights:

For questions or exception requests, open a ticket to the compliance queue and include the control_id referenced above.
